title: Parish and Portrait
premise: August Villalobos, an insurance investigator whose photographic memory has made them both invaluable and isolated, is assigned to verify the death of Father Emory Callahan, a beloved parish priest whose life policy was taken out weeks before his drowning. When a letter arrives confessing to the murder—postmarked the day after the funeral—August realizes the killer is someone with access to the case file itself, and every clue they remember points inward, toward colleagues and toward Detective Ilsa Reyes, the woman August has quietly loved for years. As August's perfect recall becomes both weapon and liability, they stage a trap using a falsified file, forcing the killer to reveal themselves: the parish's own archivist, who murdered Callahan to bury evidence that the priest had been laundering money for a powerful diocesan benefactor. In the end August must choose between turning over the full truth—which would destroy Ilsa's career for her early mishandling of the case—and protecting her, choosing love against duty while ensuring the killer still pays.
about_author: Gideon Okafor is the pen name of a former claims adjuster from Port Harcourt who spent eleven years investigating suspicious deaths before turning to fiction. They write mysteries about memory, institutions, and the quiet violence of paperwork.

chapters.title: The Weight of Water
chapters.summary: August Villalobos arrives in the river town of St. Brendan's Landing to verify the drowning death of Father Emory Callahan, whose million-dollar policy was signed six weeks prior. Through August's POV, we see their photographic memory catalog every detail of the rectory—the misplaced rosary, the dry shoes by a wet door. The emotional beat is professional detachment cracking into unease: something about this death refuses to stay filed away.

chapters.title: Postmarked Yesterday
chapters.summary: Days after closing the file, August receives a handwritten confession to Callahan's murder—postmarked the day after the funeral. In August's POV, they match the paper and ink to items photographed at the scene, realizing the writer stood inside the rectory. The beat is dread sharpening into obsession as August reopens the case alone, unable to explain why they don't report it yet.

chapters.title: The File That Remembers
chapters.summary: August compares the confession's details against the official case file and discovers facts only investigators could know—including one error only August themselves made and corrected. POV shifts to Detective Ilsa Reyes, who notices August pulling records and warns them off. The beat is wary intimacy: two people circling each other, each hiding how much they already know about the other.

chapters.title: Parish of Small Mercies
chapters.summary: August interviews the parish staff under cover of a routine audit: the anxious deacon, the grieving housekeeper, and Brother Anselm, the soft-spoken archivist who quotes the case file back to August almost verbatim. In August's POV, memory flags Anselm's phrasing as borrowed—but there's no proof. The beat is the hunter realizing the prey is watching back through the same lens.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Kept
chapters.summary: Digging into Callahan's finances, August finds the priest had been moving diocesan funds through shell accounts tied to a powerful benefactor, Monsignor Voss. Ilsa's POV reveals she was pressured months ago to close an earlier inquiry into the same accounts—a pressure she resented and obeyed. The beat is guilt and attraction entangling: August suspects Ilsa's compromise, Ilsa suspects August's silence.

chapters.title: A Second Letter
chapters.summary: A second confession arrives, this time describing August's own apartment in unsettling detail, proving the killer is surveilling them. August's POV captures the vertigo of a man with total recall being watched by someone who anticipates his every deduction. The beat is fear transmuting into resolve: August decides to stop reading the game and start playing it.

chapters.title: The Forgery
chapters.summary: August secretly builds a poisoned copy of the case file—one false detail, a fabricated witness statement placing a key figure at the rectory that night—and lets it leak through Ilsa's office. Told partly in Ilsa's POV, she catches the forgery instantly but says nothing, torn between duty and trust. The beat is love against duty made literal: she protects the trap knowing it could end her career.

chapters.title: Vespers
chapters.summary: The bait works. Anselm breaks into the records room to alter the forged page, and August confronts him among the parish archives, where Anselm reveals he killed Callahan to protect the Church—and Voss—from scandal, believing murder a form of devotion. August's POV holds the horror of a mind as ordered as his own, bent to worshipful ends. The beat is cold recognition across a shared language of detail.

chapters.title: Confession
chapters.summary: Anselm takes August hostage in the confessional, intending to stage another accident, but Isla arrives having traced the archive access logs. In alternating POV, the standoff forces both August and Ilsa to speak truths they've withheld—her buried inquiry, his concealed letters. The beat is climax as confession: Anselm surrenders not to the police but to August, asking him to 'remember it correctly.'

chapters.title: The Unfiled Page
chapters.summary: In the aftermath, Voss's network begins to unravel, and August faces the final choice: submit the complete record, which exposes Ilsa's earlier compromise, or quietly omit it. August's POV closes on him filing the truth about Anselm and Voss—but sealing Ilsa's misstep in an envelope marked for her alone, trusting her to decide. The beat is resolution as covenant: love chosen not over duty, but woven through it.
